Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0006] Read tests and sibling modules before implementing: Exploring the target file, its models, error types, and the provided tests first let the implementation match expected signatures and conventions on the first try.
  Before writing code, cat the target module, related models/money/errors modules, and any test file for the function. Then run the full test suite plus a manual edge-case script (zero, negative, float, bool, wrong state) to confirm behavior before submitting.
- [rb-0013] Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw round(): When implementing monetary functions, delegate to the repo's existing to_money/round_money helpers rather than Python's round() to match conventions and precision.
  Read sibling modules (invoice.py, money.py) to find canonical helpers like to_money and round_money, then build new pricing functions on top of them. This keeps Decimal handling and cent-rounding consistent across the codebase.
- [rb-0005] Guard bool when validating integer inputs: Python's `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `isinstance(x, int)` accepts `True`/`False`; explicitly reject bools for integer-only parameters.
  For positive-integer validation write `isinstance(quantity, bool) or not isinstance(quantity, int) or quantity <= 0`. This catches floats, strings, and booleans that would otherwise slip through or be silently coerced.
- [rb-0008] Validate numeric fields defensively before arithmetic: Guard against bool, non-int, and non-positive period values before using them in timedelta math.
  Check `isinstance(x, bool)` first (bool is an int subclass), then `isinstance(x, int)`, then `x <= 0`, raising the project's domain error. This prevents silent wrong results or TypeError from timedelta.
- [rb-0004] Reuse existing money/error helpers for validation: When implementing a billing function, delegate normalization and error signaling to the module's existing helpers rather than reimplementing them.
  Use the repo's `to_money`/`ZERO`/`round_money` helpers to normalize amounts and compare against zero, and raise the project's `BillingError(code, message)` with short machine-readable codes. This matches existing conventions and keeps error codes consistent with hidden tests.
- [rb-0010] Check idempotency key before any state validation: Money-moving operations must short-circuit on a repeated idempotency_key before validating payment state, so retries return the original result instead of raising.
  Accept keyword-only `idempotency_key=None`; first scan `audit.events(<event>)` for a matching key and return the original record unchanged. Only then validate state/amounts, and include `idempotency_key` in the audit entry you write.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw arithmetic
item.description: When implementing monetary calculations in a repo that already has money utilities, build on them rather than using floats or ad-hoc rounding.
item.content: Before writing fee/price logic, grep for existing helpers like to_money, round_money, ZERO, and error types. Importing them gives consistent validation (rejecting bool/float), correct rounding, and matching error codes for free.

item.title: Read the target file and its tests before implementing
item.description: The stub file and its test file reveal the expected signature, error behavior, and conventions.
item.content: When a task says 'add X in a new module', check whether the module already exists as a stub and read tests/test_<module>.py plus sibling modules. This surfaces required error codes, accepted input types, and import conventions before you write code.

item.title: Validate inputs via the shared converter, then check positivity
item.description: Route input through the repo's conversion helper first so type errors surface with the right codes, then enforce domain constraints like positivity.
item.content: Pattern: value = to_money(amount); if value <= ZERO: raise BillingError('non_positive_amount', repr(amount)). This separates type validation from business rules and produces distinct, testable error codes for each failure mode.
